message:
## Problem

The lastversion package had truststore support when used via the CLI (in `cli.py`), but when imported and used as a library, truststore was not initialized. This caused SSL certificate verification issues in corporate environments with custom CA certificates.

Users working in Docker environments or behind corporate firewalls encountered SSL errors when using lastversion as a library:

```python
from lastversion import latest

# This would fail with SSL certificate errors in corporate networks
# because truststore was not initialized for library usage
version = latest("some/repo")
```

The only workaround was to manually edit the lastversion source code to inject truststore, which is not a recommended practice for library users.

## Solution

This PR adds truststore initialization to `src/lastversion/__init__.py`, ensuring truststore is activated when the library is imported. This mirrors the existing approach already used in `cli.py` for CLI usage.

### Changes

**1. `src/lastversion/__init__.py`** (+8 lines)
```python
# try to use truststore if available
try:
    import truststore
    truststore.inject_into_ssl()
except ImportError:
    pass
```

**2. `setup.py`** (+1 line)
```python
extras_require={
    ...
    "truststore": ["truststore"],
}
```

## Usage

Users who need truststore support can install it as an optional dependency:

```bash
pip install lastversion[truststore]
```

For standard installation (truststore remains optional):

```bash
pip install lastversion
```

For Docker environments, the existing Dockerfile already installs truststore, and now it works for both CLI and library usage.

## Benefits

- ✅ **Works for both CLI and library usage** - No more SSL certificate errors when using lastversion as a library
- ✅ **Graceful fallback** - Works without truststore installed; it's completely optional
- ✅ **No breaking changes** - Fully backwards compatible
- ✅ **Minimal changes** - Only 9 lines added across 2 files
- ✅ **Corporate network friendly** - Automatically uses system certificate store when truststore is installed
- ✅ **Follows best practices** - Implements the recommended approach from truststore documentation

## Testing

- Verified library import works with truststore installed
- Verified graceful fallback when truststore is not available
- Confirmed CLI functionality is preserved (no regression)
- Validated package installation succeeds with and without the extra
- Passed code quality checks (flake8)

This resolves issues for users in corporate environments who need to use the system certificate store for SSL verification.

> <issue_description>I was recently trying to build a Docker image which made use of lastversion, and ran into an issue with our internal network's security certificate.   We run into this often with python and node.js utilities which do not use the system's certificate trust store.   Fortunately, with Python, there is now a package, truststore which resolves this.
> 
> As a temporary workaround, I was able to get the build working on my side by editing ```/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/lastversion/lastversion.py``` and inserting the following two lines in front of it:
> 
> ```
> import truststore
> truststore.inject_into_ssl()
> ```
> 
> That said, that's not the recommended approach for a library or package.   It would be really useful in the future if this was set up automatically by following the instructions at the bottom of the [truststore package page](https://pypi.org/project/truststore/) to set up the SSL context at the start of your requests.
> </issue_description>
